source_refs.note: Book p. 263-264: heading printed 14.1.7; properties (i)-(vi), proofs of (i)-(iv). Book error: (iii) printed u + 0 = 0. Proofs of (v), (vi), teaching notes, Key points, Common mistakes are ours.

blocks.title: Numbering note
blocks.text: The textbook prints this heading as 14.1.7 (Book# 14.1.7). The book has no 14.1.1, so the portal numbers the sub-headings of 14.1 in sequence as 14.1.1 to 14.1.8; 14.1.6 here is the book's 14.1.7.
Let \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) be vectors in the plane or in space and let \(a, b \in R\), then they have the following properties:

blocks.caption: Properties of vectors in the plane or in space, a, b real numbers

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Property (iii) is printed as \(\underline{u} + \underline{0} = \underline{0}\). Adding the zero vector leaves a vector unchanged, so it should read \(\underline{u} + \underline{0} = \underline{u}\) (Additive Identity), exactly as the book's own proof of (iii) below concludes.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
These six rules say that vectors behave like ordinary numbers for addition and for multiplying by a number. Every proof works the same way: write the vectors in components, use the matching rule for real numbers in each component, and put the components back together.
Quick numerical check of (ii) with \([1, 0, 2]\), \([3, -1, 1]\), \([0, 2, 5]\): \(([1, 0, 2] + [3, -1, 1]) + [0, 2, 5] = [4, -1, 3] + [0, 2, 5] = [4, 1, 8]\), and \([1, 0, 2] + [3, 1, 6] = [4, 1, 8]\). Same.

(i) Since for any two real numbers \(a, b \in R\), \(a + b = b + a\), it follows that for any two vectors \(\underline{u} = [x, y, z]\) and \(\underline{v} = [x', y', z']\) in \(R^{3}\), where components of \(\underline{u}\) and \(\underline{v}\) belong to \(R\):

blocks.text_alt: u plus v equals x, y, z plus x prime, y prime, z prime
equals x plus x prime and so on

blocks.latex: = [x' + x,\ y' + y,\ z' + z] \quad \because a + b = b + a
blocks.text_alt: equals x prime plus x and so on, because a plus b equals b plus a

blocks.text: So, addition of vectors in \(R^{3}\) is commutative.

(ii) Since for any three real numbers \(a, b, c \in R\), \((a + b) + c = a + (b + c)\), it follows that for any three vectors \(\underline{u} = [x, y, z]\), \(\underline{v} = [x', y', z']\) and \(\underline{w} = [x'', y'', z'']\) in \(R^{3}\), where components of \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\) and \(\underline{w}\) belong to \(R\):

blocks.latex: (\underline{u} + \underline{v}) + \underline{w} \\ = [x + x',\ y + y',\ z + z'] + [x'', y'', z'']
blocks.text_alt: u plus v, plus w, equals x plus x prime and so on, plus x double prime and so on
equals x plus x prime, plus x double prime, and so on
equals x plus, x prime plus x double prime, and so on

blocks.latex: = [x, y, z] + [x' + x'',\ y' + y'',\ z' + z''] \\ = \underline{u} + (\underline{v} + \underline{w})
blocks.text_alt: equals u plus, v plus w

blocks.text: So, addition of vectors in \(R^{3}\) is associative.

(iii) Since for any real number \(a\) and 0, \(a + 0 = a\), it follows that for any vector \(\underline{u} = [x, y, z]\) and \(\underline{0} = [0, 0, 0]\), where \(\underline{0}\) is the zero vector in \(R^{3}\):

blocks.text_alt: u plus zero vector equals x, y, z plus 0, 0, 0
equals x plus 0 and so on equals u
u plus zero vector equals u

blocks.text: Thus \(\underline{0}\) is the additive identity in \(R^{3}\).

(iv) Since for any real number \(a\), there exists \(-a\) such that \(a + (-a) = a - a = 0\), it follows that for any vector \(\underline{u} = [x, y, z]\), there exists \(-\underline{u} = [-x, -y, -z]\) in \(R^{3}\) such that

blocks.text_alt: u plus minus u equals x, y, z plus minus x, minus y, minus z
equals x plus minus x and so on
u plus minus u equals zero vector

blocks.text: Thus \(-\underline{u}\) is the additive inverse of \(\underline{u}\) in \(R^{3}\).
The proofs of the other parts are left as an exercise for the students.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Proof of (v): let \(\underline{v} = [x', y', z']\), \(\underline{w} = [x'', y'', z'']\), \(a \in R\).
\[a(\underline{v} + \underline{w}) = a[x' + x'',\ y' + y'',\ z' + z'']\]
\[= [ax' + ax'',\ ay' + ay'',\ az' + az'']\]
\[= [ax', ay', az'] + [ax'', ay'', az''] = a\underline{v} + a\underline{w}\]
The step from line 1 to line 2 uses the distributive law of real numbers, \(a(p + q) = ap + aq\), in each component.
Proof of (vi): \(a(b\underline{u}) = a[bx, by, bz] = [abx, aby, abz] = (ab)[x, y, z] = (ab)\underline{u}\), using \(a(bx) = (ab)x\) for real numbers.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Vector addition is commutative and associative.
\(\underline{0}\) is the additive identity: \(\underline{u} + \underline{0} = \underline{u}\).
\(-\underline{u}\) is the additive inverse: \(\underline{u} + (-\underline{u}) = \underline{0}\).
Scalars distribute over vector addition and multiply together: \(a(\underline{v} + \underline{w}) = a\underline{v} + a\underline{w}\), \(a(b\underline{u}) = (ab)\underline{u}\).
Each proof reduces to the same rule for real numbers in each component.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Writing \(\underline{u} + \underline{0} = \underline{0}\) (as misprinted) or writing the number 0 instead of the vector \(\underline{0}\) in \(\underline{u} - \underline{u} = \underline{0}\).
In a proof, jumping straight from \(\underline{u} + \underline{v}\) to \(\underline{v} + \underline{u}\) without showing the components: the reason lies in the components.
Forgetting to quote the real-number rule (\(\because a + b = b + a\)) that justifies the key step.
